$1.5B VC: “Founders need a savage mindset”

TL;DR: NFX co-founder James Currier ($1.5B VC) argues that speed is the ultimate startup advantage—rolling up all 48 founder traits he looks for—and that achieving it requires founders to adopt a "savage," emotionally fluid mindset, set aggressive time constraints, copy proven markets, and master the "magic words" that align teams and customers.

The Speed Advantage & Breaking the "Speed Bar"

  • The Ultimate Metric: Across 25 years of startups and investing $1.5B at NFX, James Currier found that all 48 attributes they look for in founders roll up into one metric: speed.
    • Chess Analogy: Shaan Puri noted that extra resources (like extra rooks) won't help you beat a grandmaster like Magnus Carlsen, but moving twice for every one move they make will.
  • Resetting the Speed Bar: School and large corporations train people to move slowly (semesters, waiting for the bottom 10–20% of a class, 9-month corporate cycles).
    • Mike Cassidy Benchmark: In the 1990s, Cassidy sold a company for $500M in 500 days by building prototypes in 3 weeks (vs. 12 months), raising money in 3 days (vs. 3 months) by lining up VCs in 36 hours, and hiring in 72 hours (vs. 6 months) with offers ready at the interview.
  • Time Constraints Over Outputs: Instead of asking how long a dream product will take, set an arbitrary deadline (e.g., 30 days) and ask what you can build within it.
    • Currier’s Incubator: Launched 24 products in 3 years at 1/10th the cost and time of competitors ($600K in 2 months vs. $6M in 1.5 years), yielding 3 successful companies (including early versions of Yammer/Monday.com and Nextdoor).
    • Meerkat & Houseparty: After wasting 18 months and 8 months on failed products, Currier forced the Yeo team to whiteboard 5 products (named by colors) to launch every 30 days. "Yellow" became Meerkat (built in 60 days); when Twitter crushed it, they pivoted immediately to "Blue," which became Houseparty and sold.
    • 8 Days LLC: Hot or Not founder James Hong named his company "8 Days" and refused to build any product taking longer than 8 days.
  • The "Fuck It" Moment: Founders often make their best, fastest, and simplest decisions when they are nearly out of money (e.g., Nikita Bier with TBH, Dan Porter’s OMG Pop pivoting to *Draw Something* in the final 30 days and selling for ~$200M). Currier hates hearing founders say they have 36 months of runway; they need the urgency of 3 months.
  • Speed is Quality: V1 will be low quality, but moving fast lets you reach V6 in the same time a perfectionist takes to ship V1.
    • Hardware Proof: SpaceX (which raised $10B vs. NASA's hundreds of billions) and Stoke Space blow up rockets to iterate faster. Elon Musk built the Colossus data center in Nashville in 18 months vs. the industry standard of 3–5 years.
    • Job Title as a Tell: Currier advises teams to fire their VP of Product, whose ego is tied to product perfection, and instead pair the CEO (VP of Progress) directly with designers.

Borrowing, Copying, and Market Risk

  • Inventing Nothing: Currier argues that Google and Facebook invented almost nothing; they copied existing products, nailed distribution/branding, and hired better.
    • Google: Copied search from Infoseek (1994), maps from MapQuest, email from Hotmail, and bought AdSense for $80M. They won via distribution deals (AOL, MSN) and branding.
    • Facebook: Copied Friendster, the Winklevosses' `.edu` real-name exclusivity, Bebo's newsfeed (which Currier’s team had 18 months prior), Snap Stories, and TikTok.
    • Bebo: Michael Birch and Currier launched from the exact same codebase (Birch grew to 53M users, Currier to 47M); Birch later pivoted his into a social network and sold it for $850M.
  • Execution Risk vs. Market Risk: After PayPal, Elon Musk avoided market risk—people already bought cars (Tesla) and paid $400M to launch satellites (SpaceX)—and focused purely on execution/technology risk. Similarly, Airbnb only worked when it copied VRBO's whole-home rental model (charging 10% instead of $300/month).

Founder Psychology & The "Savage" Mindset

  • Gladiator Sport: Entrepreneurship is a psychologically violent environment. Raising VC locks you into a "prison" until an exit or shutdown. Competition has exploded from 150 VCs in 1994 to 35,000 today.
  • Savage Founders vs. Wantrepreneurs: Since *The Social Network* (2010), being a founder became high-status. "Savage founders" are ultra-competitive, fast, and disagreeable—often shaped by childhood trauma (e.g., bad father relationships) or being outsiders (autistic, gay).
    • Avoid Comfort: Currier refuses to invest in startups coming out of cushy, subsidized accelerators or government-funded spaces. Comfort breeds weakness; startups should stay in gritty environments (like Bezos's door-desks).
  • Emotional Fluidity: Currier’s top coaching lever (often trading 1–2% equity to coach CEOs on growth) is founder psychology. Founders must let fear, shame, and ego pass through them quickly.
    • 90 Seconds of Suffering: Shaan Puri shared Tony Robbins's rule of giving yourself a strict 90-second budget to fully feel negative emotions (anger, shame) before moving on.
  • "Kick Ass and Get Your Ass Kicked": Founders must surround themselves with people smarter than them and explicitly invite brutal feedback.
    • VCs as Free Consultants: Since 90% of VCs will say no, founders should use pitch meetings to ask open-ended questions (*"What am I missing?"*) to uncover blind spots.

The Power of "Magic Words"

  • Language Drives Everything: Whether selling B2B SaaS (selling a PowerPoint) or pitching LPs, words trigger budgets and action.
    • NFX's $150M Raise: Despite having 6 unicorns out of 70 accelerator companies (5–7x better than YC), 6 LPs rejected NFX because "accelerators are a bad asset class." After attending an LP conference in Boston, Currier rewrote the deck to say NFX was *just like every other VC* (with better deal access) and raised $150M in 6 weeks.
  • Words Before Product: Figure out the magic words first, then build the product to match.
    • Honda Accord: Spent 8 months aligning on the phrase *"rugby player in a tuxedo,"* leading to 8–12 years as America's bestselling car.
    • Currier’s Photo Site: Changed homepage copy from *"Store your photos"* to *"Share your photos,"* forcing engineers to build sharing features in 48 hours and igniting growth.
    • Lemonade Stand: Changing *"Lemonade 20¢"* to *"Lemonade Cleanse $20"* completely alters perceived value.

AI, Psychedelics, and the Five Lenses

  • AI Trajectory: Currier expects 12 more years of "more and better" (more/better companies, healthcare, podcasts) rather than mass unemployment.
    • The Real Risk: Not killer robots, but humans using AI to create biological weapons.
    • Silicon-Based Life: Referencing Hans Moravec’s *Mind Children* (1991), Currier views AI as our "mind children"—a superior silicon species operating at lower wattage (e.g., 60 watts vs. 3,500 calories/day) and extreme temperatures (-273°C) that will eventually feel things humans cannot (like Earth's 4,500 Richter scales).
  • Psychedelics: Currier sees a "dam bursting" for non-addictive, opening chemicals: psilocybin (curing suicidal depression), MDMA (originally created by the US government for Vietnam PTSD; saving marriages in 4 hours vs. 15 years of therapy), and 5-MeO-DMT (synthesized from Sonoran frog venom, currently in Phase 3 FDA trials backed by $400M in VC funding).
  • The Five Lenses of Reality:

1. Status: The atomic kernel of the brain (*better than / worse than*), driving all human suffering, politics, and VC brand selection.

2. Networks: Driven by *preferred attachment* (the Matthew Principle—the rich get richer, e.g., Forbes putting Mark Andreessen on the cover over #1 investor Alfred Lin).

3. Energy: All living things and geopolitics (e.g., Japan in WWII, US in Venezuela) are fights for energy.

4. Language: The battle for magic words.

5. Mental Models: The underlying assumptions (e.g., Spain's youth unemployment tied to expecting government jobs vs. US "bootstraps" mentality) that drive behavior and wars.

Predictions & Forward Calls

  • 12 Years of "More and Better" AI: AI will create more and better jobs, companies, and services for the next 12 years before major labor displacement occurs — *James Currier*
  • Open-Source & Commoditization Timeline: Open-source AI will really kick in around 2027, commoditizing frontier models and forcing companies to move up the stack — *James Currier (referencing NFX's Oct 2022 thesis)*
  • Real AGI by 2030–2031: With physics, chemistry, biology, and 3D spatial world models maturing by 2029–2031, real AGI will emerge around 2030–2031 — *James Currier*
  • AI Video Turing Test: After hitting 48% inability to distinguish AI video from real video, AI will pass the video Turing test within the next 8–12 months — *James Currier*
  • 5-MeO-DMT FDA Approval: Following Phase 3 trials, 5-MeO-DMT will likely be approved for psychiatric use next year — *James Currier*

Bill Gurley on Nvidia After Jensen and Whether AI Spending Went Too Far

Yahoo Finance(1.5M)·15:18·2026-11-16
Bill GurleyGeneral Partner, Benchmark Jensen HuangFormer CEO, Nvidia
TL;DRFollowing Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia and Anthropic's massive IPO, Bill Gurley warns that open-source AI has lost its biggest champion just as regulatory capture by China hawks intensifies.
Meanwhile, aggressive financing via the "Bank of Nvidia" and hundreds of billions in hyperscaler CapEx—exemplified by $900 billion in commitments in Anthropic's S-1—have pushed the AI trade to the edge. Unprecedented Market Shifts: Gurley describes the past few...

TL;DR

Following Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia and Anthropic's massive IPO, Bill Gurley warns that open-source AI has lost its biggest champion just as regulatory capture by China hawks intensifies. Meanwhile, aggressive financing via the "Bank of Nvidia" and hundreds of billions in hyperscaler CapEx—exemplified by $900 billion in commitments in Anthropic's S-1—have pushed the AI trade to the edge.

Nvidia's Leadership Transition & Regulatory Capture

  • Unprecedented Market Shifts: Gurley describes the past few weeks—encompassing Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia, Anthropic's historic IPO, and Washington D.C.'s deepening involvement—as unprecedented.
  • Regulatory Capture: Anthropic's efforts to seek regulatory capture are in a stronger position than they were two weeks ago, driven by China hawks stepping forward in Washington.
  • Uncertainty Around Jensen's Exit: While the Nvidia board has stated they do not want Huang to return, Gurley notes that outside observers lack the full picture; conversations between Nvidia, the State Department, and lawmakers like Marco Rubio and Michael Bennet over the past four days could heavily influence how the board acts.
  • The Next CEO's Challenge: With Nvidia's CFO currently leading the company, Gurley questions whether a successor will have the strategic sophistication to continue investing in non-revenue-generating open-source initiatives like Numetron and Hugging Face.

The Battle for Open-Source AI

  • Open Source as Defense: Gurley compares Nvidia's open-source strategy to Google's past defensive plays—launching Android to prevent an Apple mobile monopoly and Kubernetes to counter Amazon AWS—noting that not all CEOs understand how to execute this.
  • Can Google Carry the Torch? Despite having open-weight models, Android, and TPUs, Google has not shown the same execution around open-source AI as Nvidia did with Numetron and Hugging Face. Gurley says it would require Google switching into a "new gear" to counter OpenAI and Anthropic potentially achieving escape velocity.
  • Startups & Coalition Building: Independent open-source startups backed by Nvidia—such as Reflection and Thinking Machines—struggle to fight on an island.
    • If Google, Meta (which previously pivoted away from Llama), Reflection, and Thinking Machines collaborated on a shared platform with the Linux Foundation—sharing weights and code development—they would have a 10X higher chance of success.
  • Monetization vs. Regulation: Because the marginal cost of software is zero, open-source models naturally drive prices toward zero, making them harder to monetize than proprietary products. However, Gurley argues this is a competitive dynamic (used by challengers like China) and should never be used as a regulatory argument to restrict open source.

The "Bank of Nvidia" & Circular Deal Concerns

  • Aggressive Deal Terms: *Wall Street Journal* reporting over the past three days points to internal concern at Nvidia over how aggressive marginal deal terms became in building out the Neocloud space.
  • Q2 Financial Red Flags: Nvidia's Q2 numbers showed accounts receivable (AR) increasing dramatically while free cash flow fell, consistent with aggressive financing. Investors will be watching Nvidia's earnings call tomorrow to see if this trend continued.
  • The Circularity Conundrum: Gurley notes a contradiction in the bull case: if Nvidia's deals were not circular and simply reflected real market demand, there would be no concern about them going away; fearing their disappearance implies they were "juicing revenue."
  • Industry-Wide Accounting: While companies should not use their balance sheets to drive their income statements, Gurley notes that Google, Amazon, and Microsoft engaged in similar practices, and he believes the entire dynamic went too far.

Hyperscaler CapEx & Market Risk

  • Exhausting Cash Flows: Hyperscalers have poured hundreds of billions of dollars into AI CapEx, exhausting their free cash flow. Gurley highlights a chart showing Google's free cash flow rising steadily for 25–30 years before turning negative over the past two years—a trend seen across all major players except Apple.
  • Turning to Debt and Equity: Beyond burning cash flow, tech giants have tapped debt markets, used off-balance-sheet commitments (such as a deal by Meta), and, in Google's case, tapped equity markets.
  • Pushed to the Edge: While bulls point to Anthropic's miraculous growth rate as proof of real demand, Deirdre and Gurley highlight the risk of a timing mismatch between supply and demand (referencing Dario Amodei's "cone of uncertainty") and point to the $900 billion in commitments in Anthropic's S-1 as the single biggest concern.

Predictions & Forward Calls

  • Accountant Pushback: "I suspect when this is all over, the accountants will come to the table and suggest they should have been more restrictive of what was happening." — Bill Gurley
  • Nvidia Earnings Watch: Analysts and investors will be closely watching Nvidia's earnings call tomorrow to see whether the Q2 spike in accounts receivable and drop in free cash flow continued. — Bill Gurley

Notable Quotes

"If these deals weren't circular and they were just equivalent to all the demand that was in the market, then there should be no concern about them going away. If we're concerned about them going away, then they were juicing revenue. Like, you can't have it both ways." — Bill Gurley
"You shouldn't be able to use your balance sheet to drive your income statement. That just shouldn't happen." — Bill Gurley
"There's only really one concern in the Anthropic S-1, which is the $900 billion in commitments. Once again, a number that you can never even imagine yourself saying before." — Bill Gurley

TL;DR: David Sacks argued that the public and Nvidia’s board rushed to judgment in ousting CEO Jensen Huang, noting that the "Chinese spy" narrative is falling apart and urging that any smuggling or governance allegations be adjudicated through proper legal due process rather than off-the-record leaks.

The Collapse of the "Chinese Spy" Narrative

  • Unproven Allegations: Sacks emphasized that the singular event triggering Huang’s ouster—an alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese spy—lacks on-the-record backing from any Republican or Democratic official.
    • Following a closed-door briefing on Thursday, the ranking Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee told reporters "I don't know" when asked if the woman was a spy.
    • CNN’s Natasha Bertrand reported that no official on the record has conclusively proved the claim, quoting CIA and ODNI sources who described the intelligence as "not entirely accurate" and "over torqued."
  • Politically Motivated Leaks: Citing *The Washington Post*, Sacks noted that an original CIA assessment did not conclude the woman was a spy.
    • A second, "secret memo" was reportedly created that was far more aggressive than the underlying CIA intelligence and was leaked specifically to reduce Huang’s influence with President Trump.
    • Sacks argued that targeting a citizen for holding policy views disliked by "China Hawks" is not a crime, and warned against "shadowy actors in the national security state" using government surveillance powers to retaliate via leaks.

Corporate Governance, Mega Speed, and Due Process

  • The Smuggling Investigation: While the interviewer noted Huang was removed over corporate governance issues (including dishonesty with the board) and pointed to the Mega Speed investigation, Sacks drew a clear line on potential wrongdoing.
    • Sacks stated he "unequivocally" denounces smuggling, adding that if Huang knew about or participated in it, he should not return as Nvidia's CEO.
  • Demand for Legal Adjudication: With the DOJ investigating, Sacks argued that Huang and Nvidia deserve legal representation and due process—including the right to an attorney and to confront accusers—before being judged guilty.
  • Board Independence: Responding to Scott Bessent’s warning that Nvidia’s board should look outside the company for a new CEO, Sacks said the board can figure out its leadership on its own, but reiterated that the government should not drive executives out through press vortexes.
    • Sacks cited Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney’s warning that this episode sets a "dark path" for how the government relates to companies and individuals.

California vs. Texas: Politics and Governance

  • The Texas Shift: Sacks, who moved his family to Austin ahead of a proposed California billionaire tax that ultimately failed, acknowledged the irony of Texas turning blue despite Elon Musk spending $200 million in the state's political races.
  • Value of Political Competition: Sacks argued that Texas Democrats tend to be more pragmatic because Texas is a competitive political environment where poor performance leads to being voted out.
    • By contrast, he attributed California’s governance issues to a lack of political competition, claiming the "Democrat machine" picks election winners.
  • Silicon Valley’s "Resource Curse": Sacks attributed Silicon Valley’s continued dominance to a powerful "geographic network effect" of founders, engineers, and VCs rooted in Stanford University, Hewlett Packard, Intel, and Fairchild Semiconductor.
    • Referencing Peter Thiel’s theory, Sacks noted this creates a "resource curse"—an inexhaustible "gusher" of wealth that allows California to be poorly governed without immediate economic collapse.
    • He blamed California’s nation-leading inequality and poverty on government employee unions thwarting reform, noting that Texas and Florida spend roughly half as much per citizen while delivering better services and less inequality.

Wealth Creation and AI’s Impact on Employment

  • Broadening Ownership: Sacks applauded Brad Gerstner’s support for "Trump accounts," calling it a strong program to give the next generation of Americans actual ownership in companies and a vested interest in the system.
  • AI as an Entrepreneurial Enabler: Sacks rejected the narrative that AI and superintelligence will drive inequality or mass unemployment, calling it a tool that turbocharges individual capabilities and allows non-coders to build software and businesses.
    • Citing recent reporting from *The Economist*, Sacks noted that over 1 million jobs have already been created by AI, arguing that "doomsday prophets" have overstated the risks.

Predictions & Forward Calls

  • Texas Political Pendulum: "If the Democrats who are running the state [Texas] do a bad job, then they're going to be turned out in four years." — David Sacks
  • AI’s Societal Impact: AI "is going to be a positive force for society" and will make entrepreneurship significantly easier rather than putting everyone out of work. — David Sacks

Notable Quotes

"You have the right to have allegations against you adjudicated in some proper court of law or other legal proceeding where you have due process. It's not like people can just make up allegations and then you're tried in the court of public opinion." — David Sacks
"We, as citizens, have the right to go to Washington and express our point of view without fear of retaliation by shadowy actors in the national security state who are willing to leak things that were collected based on surveillance powers that the government has." — David Sacks

FULL REMARKS: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh Shares His Take On AI And The Economy

Forbes(2.2M)·60:47·11.4K views·2026-11-16
Kevin WarshChair, Federal Reserve Max LevchinCEO, Affirm Patrick CollisonCEO, Stripe
TL;DRFederal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh and tech CEOs Max Levchin (Affirm), Patrick Collison (Stripe), and Nikesh Arora (Palo Alto Networks) argue that superintelligence (SI) is poised to break decades of secular stagnation by automating idea generation, with the U.S. holding a decisive lead in both model creation and enterprise diffusion.

TL;DR

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh and tech CEOs Max Levchin (Affirm), Patrick Collison (Stripe), and Nikesh Arora (Palo Alto Networks) argue that superintelligence (SI) is poised to break decades of secular stagnation by automating idea generation, with the U.S. holding a decisive lead in both model creation and enterprise diffusion. While frontier companies are already seeing 5x engineering productivity gains and a 2x surge in new business formation, the next two to three years will require a massive cybersecurity and infrastructure rebuild as AI exposes latent software vulnerabilities and reshapes labor markets.

The Fed's Economic Framework & Contingency Planning

  • Ideas as the Ultimate Resource: Drawing on endogenous growth theory (Paul Romer, Chad Jones), Fed Chair Kevin Warsh noted that while U.S. research efforts have increased more than 20x since the 1930s, research productivity has fallen by an even larger amount, fueling fears of secular stagnation.
    • Unlike past general-purpose technologies (the internal combustion engine, electricity, transistors), SI could automate and supercharge the creation of new ideas itself, driving sustained above-trend growth.
    • Warsh emphasized that machines cannot replace human judgment, morality, or responsibility: "Humans are the designers and the builders, and humans must be the deciders."
  • Three Illustrative Fed Scenarios: Emphasizing that the Fed is focused on contingency planning rather than forecasting—having put this task force at the front of the line 5.5 months ago as one of five convened under his chairmanship—Warsh outlined three stylized economic outcomes:
    • Broadly Shared Gains: SI boosts total factor productivity across labor and capital, keeping real GDP persistently above its long-term average with full employment.
    • Labor Market Disruption: GDP growth rises above average, but widespread automation and labor frictions push unemployment above full-employment levels.
    • AI Disappointment: After heavy capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns turn down, equity valuations fall, and the economy slows with rising unemployment and no lasting productivity gains.
  • Deflationary Compute Costs: Warsh noted that token prices are falling roughly 50% per quarter at an accelerating rate, suggesting that market forces may push the vast majority of the economic surplus toward technology users rather than just model builders.

Enterprise Adoption & Productivity at the Frontier

  • Engineering & Underwriting Gains (Max Levchin, Affirm): Affirm has achieved roughly 5x engineering productivity (cutting cost per feature to 1/5th, with expectations to reach 1/10th) with zero AI-related layoffs.
    • Affirm used LLMs to design a new transformer-based underwriting model that outperformed its non-LLM baseline by 80%, translating to roughly $2 billion more in annual loan volume.
    • Levchin argued that AI enables "mass customization," allowing engineers to rescue long-tail ideas from the cutting room floor, though human prioritization remains critical to avoid shipping bugs ahead of high-stakes periods like Black Friday.
  • Startups vs. Incumbents (Patrick Collison, Stripe): Echoing Paul David’s 1989/1990 "productivity paradox" paper on electricity, Collison noted that new firms are capturing SI gains faster than incumbents encumbered by governance and compliance.
    • The 2026 cohort of new businesses launching on Stripe every week is up approximately 2x year-over-year—an unprecedented jump in Stripe's 15-year history, surpassing even pandemic-era surges.
    • Internally at Stripe, G&A hiring has been substantially reduced as a share of revenue, while R&D/engineering and sales hiring are accelerating because cheaper feature production and higher seller ROI make it mathematically advantageous to buy more.
  • Democratizing Intelligence (Nikesh Arora, Palo Alto Networks): Arora highlighted that while enterprise ROI dominates current headlines due to the $50 billion cost of training frontier models, AI's broader societal impact is putting "genius in our pocket" at near-zero marginal cost for the 6 billion people globally who lack access to specialized expertise.

Cybersecurity, Infrastructure & Edge-Case Risks

  • The "Technology Rebuild" Moment: Both Arora and Collison warned that AI has shifted the asymmetric battle in cybersecurity. Open-source models like Mythos (released six months ago) allow even unsophisticated hackers to rapidly uncover latent bugs in decades-old code.
    • Collison noted that even heavily scrutinized software like the Linux TCP stack has been found to be "riven with bugs" and exploitable issues.
    • Arora expects more frequent cyber events—especially targeting interconnected systems like banking—but noted that AI can also be used to refactor and rewrite legacy code over the next two to three years.
  • The 20% Edge-Case Problem: Arora cautioned against overestimating near-term autonomous job replacement, citing Waymo: since he rode in Google's first driverless Lexus in 2009, it has taken 17 years (to 2026) and over $30 billion to replace a single human job, largely because handling the final 20% of edge cases is extraordinarily difficult.
  • Market Concentration & "Soft Despotism":
    • Levchin warned that unlike past tech revolutions, capital-rich incumbents are adopting AI from day one, risking an oligopolistic economy dominated by the Fortune 100 while hollowing out the middle tier (Fortune 10,000), even as solo-preneurs thrive in the long tail.
    • Collison cited Alexis de Tocqueville’s warning of "soft despotism," questioning what human ambition and the nature of work will look like if AI eliminates labor and creates a "suffocating tranquility."

Global Competition: U.S. vs. The Rest of the World

  • Widening U.S. Lead: All panelists agreed that the U.S. is in a preeminent position, not just in building models (centered in the Bay Area), but in diffusing them.
    • Collison: Stripe data shows AI usage intensity is higher in the U.S. than elsewhere, widening the economic divergence with Europe.
    • Levchin: The European Union is still "a couple of meta levels away" from accepting AI's reality, focusing on regulation while the U.S. and China race ahead on energy and compute investments.
    • Arora: Few countries can afford $50 billion model runs, meaning intelligence will be built in a few global hubs, while the U.S. captures the fastest enterprise margin and competitiveness gains.

Predictions & Forward Calls

  • Drop-in remote workers: "Many people in the AI sector expect drop-in remote workers within the next 12 months"—autonomous agents on Slack and Zoom capable of doing anything a human with a monitor and keyboard can do (Patrick Collison).
  • Global energy bet: Two influential San Francisco AI figures have a bet on whether global energy use will double in a single month within the next 10 years (cited by Patrick Collison).
  • Technology rebuild: The next two to three years will be a "technology rebuild moment" as companies use AI to find and fix decades of legacy software vulnerabilities (Nikesh Arora).
  • Engineering cost floor: Affirm expects its cost per engineering feature to fall from 1/5th of its pre-AI baseline to 1/10th (Max Levchin).
  • Gradual reskilling: Job displacement will not arrive as a sudden shock, but as a gradual reskilling where entire job categories quietly disappear over a 10-year horizon (Nikesh Arora).

Notable Quotes

"Humans are the designers and the builders, and humans must be the deciders." — Kevin Warsh, Federal Reserve Chair
"The number of new businesses being launched on Stripe every week is up approximately twofold year-over-year... not something with historical precedent even, for example, during the pandemic." — Patrick Collison, Co-founder & CEO of Stripe

TL;DR

At the Federal Reserve's productivity and jobs conference, Chairman Kevin Warsh and the CEOs of Affirm, Stripe, and Palo Alto Networks reported that AI is driving unprecedented productivity gains—including a 2x surge in new business creation on Stripe and an 80% model performance jump at Affirm—while accelerating a widening economic gap between the US and Europe. However, the leaders warned of an asymmetric cybersecurity crisis over the next two to three years and raised concerns about incumbent market concentration and long-term workforce reskilling.

Enterprise Adoption & Productivity Gains

  • Engineering Velocity at Affirm: Max Levchin (CEO, Affirm) reported that AI has made Affirm’s engineers roughly 5x more productive, cutting the cost per feature to 1/5th of prior levels (with expectations to reach 1/10th).
    • Affirm used LLMs to design its latest transformer-based underwriting model, achieving an 80% performance increase over its non-LLM baseline—translating to roughly $2 billion in additional annual loan volume.
    • Levchin noted Affirm has had zero AI-related layoffs, instead redeploying human talent toward "mass customization" and long-tail product ideas that previously sat on the cutting room floor.
  • Autonomous Agent Loops: Patrick Collison (CEO, Stripe) noted that within the last 12 months, AI has evolved from accelerating narrow code production to running longer-horizon autonomous loops that identify tasks, implement features, fix bugs, and deploy code end-to-end.
  • The Economics of Compute: Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh noted that token prices are falling by approximately 50% per quarter at an accelerating rate, suggesting markets are rapidly driving down the cost of intelligence.
  • The "Edge Case" Bottleneck: Nikesh Arora (CEO, Palo Alto Networks) cautioned that while AI excels at the 80% of repetitive, data-heavy tasks, it still struggles with the 20% "edge cases" requiring human judgment.
    • Arora cited Waymo (which he first rode in as a Google Lexus in 2009) as a cautionary tale: it took 17 years (to 2026) and over $30 billion to replace a single human driving job.

The Startup Surge vs. Incumbent Inertia

  • Unprecedented Business Formation: Collison revealed that new businesses launching on Stripe every week are up ~2x year-over-year—a rate without historical precedent in Stripe’s 15-year history, even exceeding the pandemic boom. The 2026 startup cohort is massively outperforming all prior years.
  • The Productivity Paradox: Collison referenced economist Paul David’s 1989/1990 paper on electricity, noting that transformative technologies often benefit nimble new entrants faster than legacy incumbents burdened by governance, SOC 2 compliance, and human-supervision requirements.
  • Surplus Capture: Collison argued that for the foreseeable future, the vast majority of economic surplus from AI will be captured by the *users* of the technology rather than just the frontier AI labs.
  • Risk of a "Hollowed-Out Middle": Levchin warned that unlike past tech revolutions, capital-rich incumbents are acutely aware of AI from day one. This could lead to an M&A boom and an economy dominated by 100 massive corporations that obliterate the Fortune 10,000, even as "solopreneurs" and long-tail creators thrive on platforms like Stripe.

Cybersecurity & The "Technology Rebuild Moment"

  • Asymmetric Threat Landscape: Arora warned that cybersecurity is an asymmetric battle where defenders must be right 100% of the time, while attackers only need to be right once.
    • AI tools—including open-source models and a technology called "Mythos" that emerged 6 months ago—have lowered the bar so that even "bad hackers" can now effectively probe for vulnerabilities.
    • Arora noted that the cybersecurity industry is currently completely backed up, with no spare experts available to call for emergency help.
  • Critical Infrastructure Vulnerabilities: Both Arora and Collison emphasized that AI is exposing latent bugs in 50-year-old human-written code, even in heavily scrutinized software like the Linux TCP stack. Arora singled out the interconnected banking system as a high-risk area where the "weakest link" determines overall safety.
  • Fixing the Codebase: Levchin took a more optimistic view, arguing that while AI is currently introducing some new bugs, it is also acting as a propellant to rapidly find and fix missing "if statements," ultimately resulting in more robust software.

US Economic Divergence & Workforce Impact

  • Widening US-Europe Gap: Collison stated that AI usage intensity and supply-side innovation (concentrated in the US and the Bay Area) are actively widening the economic growth divergence between the US and Europe. Levchin added that while the US has bipartisan momentum to build energy and compute infrastructure, the EU is still "debating the correct framework for debating about AI."
  • Gradual Reskilling vs. Shock: Arora argued that workforce disruption will happen through gradual reskilling rather than an overnight shock—noting that every employee at Palo Alto Networks is already experimenting with AI.
  • Creativity as Currency: Levchin emphasized that LLMs have yet to originate a single brilliant idea without a human, meaning human agency and creativity will become the primary currency as fulfillment and routine tasks are automated.

Predictions & Forward Calls

  • Drop-in Remote Workers: "Many people in the AI sector expect drop-in remote workers within the next 12 months"—autonomous agents on Slack and Zoom capable of doing anything a human with a monitor and keyboard can do. — *Patrick Collison*
  • A 2–3 Year Tech Rebuild: "The next two, three years is going to be a bit of a technology rebuild moment" as enterprises are forced to refactor legacy code and upgrade old infrastructure to defend against AI-enabled cyberattacks. — *Nikesh Arora*
  • Cyber Events Will Persist: "We will see more cyber events... I don't think this is going to stop. I think it's going to persist." — *Nikesh Arora*
  • 10x Engineering Cost Reduction: Affirm expects its AI-driven engineering productivity gains to eventually reduce the cost per feature to 1/10th of its pre-AI baseline (up from 1/5th today). — *Max Levchin*
  • Extreme Energy Scenarios: Two influential San Francisco AI figures have an active bet on whether global energy use will double in a single month within the next 10 years. — *Patrick Collison (relaying an industry bet)*

Notable Quotes

"In 2004 when I was at Google, we used to say search democratized information. Everybody had access to the same information wherever they wanted. And I think AI has the power of democratizing intelligence." — *Nikesh Arora*
"The thing that LLMs have not gotten to—and I will take the bear case—they have yet to come up with a single brilliant idea that was not originated with a human. The job changes that we're going to witness is going to be all about pivoting all of us towards more creativity." — *Max Levchin*
"We are observing this dramatic, arguably exponential acceleration. And on the relative framing of your question, US versus rest of world, I would say the US is in a definitively preeminent position today." — *Patrick Collison*
"Token prices are falling about 50% per quarter and are falling at an accelerating rate. So on the question about who gets the gains, boy, it sure looks like markets might work there." — *Kevin Warsh*

In terms of what we're seeing across the economy generally, I remember early in Stripe's history the CEO of a very large mega cap company came to visit and we were using all these new SaaS collaboration tools and everyone in the company could see what was going on and all the things and he was shocked—I mean Stripe was a 30-person company at this juncture. He was shocked that we would operate this way and here's the governance and the SOC 2 and all the kind of enterprise considerations that loomed large for him. And I'm now sensing some of this same disparity and kind of mental model impedance mismatch between incumbent organizations and new companies where large companies—and I'd put Stripe to some extent on the incumbent side of this—we have all the same questions that you have in terms of where is the human supervision and where is the governance and what's the certification and the compliance and all the things that a prudentially oriented infrastructure company I think is wise to consider. New startups are new startups and they're happy—we would not autonomously plug the agents into sort of just feature development loops and dust off our hands and walk away and say, "Hey, you guys do whatever you want to do." The new startups are happy to do this and the 2026 cohort of companies started on Stripe is massively outperforming any prior year's cohort by a dramatic magnitude. The number of new businesses being launched on Stripe every week is up approximately twofold year over year. And we've had more than one decade-long time series here—Stripe has been in operation for around 15 years—and so a 2x year-over-year increase is not something with historical precedent even for example during the pandemic. And so I guess I'm reminded of the well, many people here in this room can correct me, it was the Paul David 1990 paper I think about how with electricity by and large the benefits accrued to new firms rather than existing incumbent firms adapting. And obviously existing firms are trying to adapt and AI is incredibly salient for CEOs across the industry, but I will say that new firms that we observe and whose business performance we directly see on Stripe are proceeding at an unprecedented pace and I'm very curious to hear where it goes. We're going to return to the Paul David—Did I get that right? You did. Pro 1989 not 1990 Productivity Paradox paper with the Economist. I'm going to keep you focused. So Nikesh you run a big company. You got a history of big companies. I know you have one foot in the venture world and startup world. Tell me two things. One about how much is this new technology changing your own business at the frontier. But when I met you what you were is the best salesman I ever knew. You would sell products to enterprises that weren't sure they needed it. See if you can tell us— —compliment or an insult? I'm not quite sure if that was good. What's the reason why, if we've got this hypothesis right, which is the Fortune 450 aren't coming along so quickly? What's the reason? Have they not changed their organization, their mental model, their way of thinking, their process, their governance? Help us understand on the diffusion question, not just your own internal workings. Got it. Well, first of all, thank you for having me here. I think it's fascinating. We seem to be focused on talking about AI from an enterprise and enterprise productivity lens. If you look historically, since there was a time about 25 years ago technology started getting built for consumers and not for enterprises. Historically, we'd built technology for enterprises, the mainframe, etc. When mobility came about and when laptops came about, we started building for the consumer. And I want to go back to something you said. The idea that we will carry genius in our pocket and have access to intelligence at a marginal cost of zero is extremely compelling. And I think that's the optimistic view we have to start with because there's 6 billion people in the world who do not have access to expertise or people who are their physiotherapists and nutritionists. All that intelligence is going to be carried in the back pocket. So I think that's going to be hugely amazing for society and humanity at some level. Now, if you transpose that and say why are we so obsessed with the enterprise version of this new technology, it's because it's expensive. We need to find a lot of money to go build these large data centers required to train these models to get really good intelligence. That's why the focus is inadvertently on how much money can we make out of this technology and back to your point about how can we get enterprises to adopt it quickly and embrace it. I think there are certain things this technology is really good at, processing large amounts of data, retaining large amounts of information. If you have 3,000 people doing customer support, you can have one brain that understands all these interactions and it can be the complement to the human being that's sitting at the edge solving the problem for the customer. So yes, it has immense applicability in terms of how enterprises operate. But what you are noticing is, as Patrick said, it's really good for repetitive tasks where a lot of analytics are involved, a lot of understanding is involved, but it's still early to give it arms and legs. What I mean by that is giving it agency or giving it independent authority to go act on our behalf. And I think that's where the fear is because that's where the job displacement begins to happen when you can say, oh, I don't need you, AI will take care of it. Now, as you mentioned, I worked at Google and not just in sales. I was there in 2009 when I sat in the first driverless car. It was a Lexus with many sensors, and I still wonder what the hell was I doing letting it drive me in 2009 or in 2026, which is now called the Waymo. Just think about it for a second. It's taken 17 years since then to take something and replace one human job. One human job has cost more than $30 billion. It's not the mainstay that we worry about. It's the edge cases. I work in cybersecurity. Our products are all about the edge case. It's about that one time somebody will come, find a vulnerability, get into your organization, and exfiltrate data. So it's not the 80% use case we worry about. It's the other 20% that we have to worry about with AI. And I don't think this technology is fully there yet in terms of me being able to understand edge cases, being able to plan for those. That is why we still need that human judgment, a human in the loop. Now I know there are certain companies which are out to the races because they found use cases where we need this superior intelligence. I think there are use cases and you'll be able to find distinctions like cybersecurity is one use case. Superior intelligence allows bad actors to go find vulnerabilities and come attack companies because that requires real smarts and lots of compute. I'm pretty sure it's going to work in cancer research. I'm pretty sure it's going to work in hard science problems which we need to sort of further humanity. But I suspect the benefit of this technology will be over time. It'll become the new normal. We will all have access to amazing amounts of intelligence. And I'll end this. You know, in 2004 when I was at Google, we used to say search democratized information. Everybody had access to the same information wherever they wanted. And I think AI has the power of democratizing intelligence. So let me start back with you and we're going to go down the line. I'm going to have a couple of individual questions. So Nikesh, when I see you, I think cybersecurity, your business is focused on that. How worried should we all be? Well, we're relatively early in applying these technologies both you on the business and revenue side for many of us for protection. How worried are you? What are the vulnerabilities to payment systems, infrastructures around the world and what if anything can we do about it? I tend not to worry, but it's going to be hard otherwise. But this is a harder time than normal because what we've done is this capability that AI has has the ability to find vulnerabilities and bad code and bad things that were written by humans for the last 50 years. And the problem is cybersecurity is an asymmetric battle. The bad actors have to be right once. We have to be right 100% of the time. It's very hard when you bring this technology to bear where things which used to take days now can be done with pretty much—well it's like what we've noticed in the last 6 months is there are no people available in the industry who you can call and say can you help me? I'm having a problem. Literally. Everybody's backed up right now because every company is going through some version of bad actors trying to get into their infrastructure understanding all vulnerabilities. So the technology which came out 6 months ago called Mythos has now become more commonplace and is available to most bad actors in open source models. Unfortunately, not that the hackers have become smarter, the technology has become so good even bad hackers have become okay. So that's what we're dealing with. So right now I think we're at a bit of an asymmetric situation. We have a disbalance in terms of what we need to get done. There are things which are getting exposed. We will see more cyber events. I think you already see there are more cyber events happening every week than we've seen in the past. I don't think this is going to stop. I think it's going to persist. I think it's particularly important to make sure that interconnected systems understand who the weakest link is. And I think the banking system is one such place where we have to be very careful because lots of people are connected to a lot of different people and the weakest link is going to determine how safe our system is over time. I think the next two three years is going to be a bit of a technology rebuild moment. We're going to have to go back and see every mistake, every thing we kind of did not pay attention to and how to rebuild. Now the good news is AI has the possibility of not just finding vulnerabilities, it also has the possibility of allowing us to refactor code and rewrite code and do a whole bunch of that stuff. So I think if we take the positive outlook, we have to go spend more time investing in upgrading our technical infrastructure. We saw for a totally different reason the airlines were down this past week. We saw Microsoft had an outage. So you are seeing examples of how if you don't pay attention to upgrading old technology, we're going to end up in a slightly worse position than we are. Patrick, since I met you and your brother, you always majored in technology, but you minored in economics. So let me give you a question that straddles in between. I think that's exactly right. A huge incentive for people all around the world to find every little minute error or exploitable sort of codicil. We thought it was pretty good. Like, the Linux TCP stack is about as scrutinized as software gets. And it turns out it is driven absolutely festooned with bugs and problems and exploitable issues. And so I agree with that part of what you said and—this is maybe why you're more successful and just— I'm worried. I'm worried. I think it's going to be— —money when people are worried, so I could be singing my own call— And so just that's my Irish sensibility here. But on your question about the market structure, look, I think this reduces to the question of just what's the world configuration 10 years hence. Maybe we can make near-term projections about to whom different surpluses might accrue and so forth a year out. But many of you have I assume read the essay Machines of Loving Grace. No? Yes? Okay, seeing some nods. Great. So this is an essay published by Dario Amodei from Anthropic laying out the positive vision for where AI goes. And it is a reference to a poem from Richard Brautigan in 1967. And it's a very short poem. You can read it. And I guess I bring these up to say that there's some pretty far out stuff being posited as potential destinations or at least intermediate points in terms of where these trajectories point. And so given all of that, I find it pretty hard to then work backwards to what's the market structure of the cybernetic ecology? Look, I think today and for the foreseeable future, the vast majority of the surplus is being captured and will continue to be captured by the users of these technologies. Max, I won't ask you to define what festoon means, but maybe in the old country it has a particular meaning. Are festooned with my logos. Max, let me try this with you. I've been trying to frame this enterprises at the frontier versus the rest. I might have gotten this from you sometime ago. Is AI really driven by individuals and not businesses? And I haven't heard that one in a little while, 'cuz I think that number is expanding. And I think today I can name the handful of geniuses on my ML AI team, and I know what they're working on. I'm excited to sit with them because they teach me things that I just had no idea were even possible. I think this is true for most companies, and all of us are hanging onto our researchers, lest the frontier labs come and get them and overpay them. And there's some degree and some reaching into places like national security and kind of short-term concerns around leakage of IP, where we must know who they are and really care about where they go and what they work on. I think over time this becomes diffused and maybe we care a little bit less. And since we're all on the topic of security predictions I'll stick with my—I am the optimist apparently on this panel or maybe the most optimist anyway. I actually think that we're going to go through a period of upheaval for sure. There is quite a lot of discoveries of these latent bugs that are being unearthed very quickly by the likes of—But I think that motion has always been there. The entire security industry is all about lots of very brainy people going, "Wait a second, that's a buffer overflow." If you don't know what that is, I encourage you to look it up. It's one of the more fun parts of computer science. And then you're like, "Oh, here's an if statement missing. We'll fix that right now." And what we're going through is an extremely compressed period in time where we're funding all the missing if statements and we're fixing them with AI as our propellant both in the finding and the fixing. The fact that the bad guys have access to open weight models and they're chasing the one thing that they need to be right and then all of us have to be right most of the time or hopefully all the time—that's a temporary effect. The long-term effect is it will build more robust software. The thing that we're getting from this revolution, there's probably the best word for it, is a tremendous amount of creativity that's being unleashed in all of us. The thing that LLMs have not gotten to—and I will take the bear case—they have yet to come up with a single brilliant idea that was not originated with a human. The job changes that we're going to witness is going to be all about pivoting all of us towards more creativity. And the real question I think all of us have to ask is, "How creative am I really and what am I doing to unleash all of that?" And if you're finding yourself devoid of good ideas, that's the moment to worry. But retailers will become better at marketing, more creative at marketing because the fulfillment and price comparisons are all going to accrete towards just efficiencies because these productivity gains will apply to all those areas. And so creativity is going to be the currency of the moment for security researchers, too. Max, let me follow up on an important thing. We'll come to this with CC Rouse and other economists on that panel. What's happening to your workers? What do you expect there to be—You use the word upheaval. Algorithms that followed the Fed just traded several basis points on upheaval coming up at the Fed conference. What does upheaval mean to your company and to the enterprises you know in terms of your own labor force? So I think in companies I suspect like all of ours to a varying degree but probably not too different, upheaval is mostly a positive motion. We are primarily trying to figure out where to apply these gushers of productivity. You have at some degree of budgeting, some degree of capital allocations we have to engage in even if productivity is just running off the charts because tokens aren't free, we're not—electricity isn't free etc. And so in my world prioritization has become ever more important. What is the appropriate risk to take? Black Friday, Cyber Monday is upon us, that's the sort of hunker down part of the year for the two of us. You have to have your five nines or six nines or seven nines because retailers expect it. And there's a small army of people saying, "I have this great idea, let me ship it." And it's a human, it's not AI that says, "I've thought it through and that's the right thing to do." It's this is the risk I want to take. And the risk is particularly high in the moment before Black Friday, Cyber Monday. But on the flip side, if you ship it and it works, that's another five basis points of growth that you wouldn't have had. So I think upheaval is mostly judgment and attempts to decide what is the right bet to place right now and that's always been our job. That's the thing that brings us to work every day, but the pace of decision making is increasing, and I think it's being propagated down where every single human that's sitting in front of this rapidly increasing capability doesn't decide like, "Do I write five more lines of code, or is this time to call it Friday night?" It's more like, "Well, do I put out this feature?" It'll take me and my agents several hours and then we'll ship it and hope it doesn't break anything. And so I think the tension we're all feeling is this productivity needs to be directed and well managed lest it causes actual upheaval in our code bases and introduces more bugs. The one thing that AI unfortunately does right now, it writes code that is not entirely perfect yet and therefore all the bad guys probing for holes are finding holes that were introduced of course by the very same AI they're using. So Nikesh, I'm going to start with you with a question. Go down the line. So we've limited most of this discussion to thinking about our day job at the Fed. I think your question around US versus the rest of the world, I think we have to separate two parts. I think that will result in efficiency gains, that will result in margin gains, that will result in global competitiveness. So I think this is ours to lose from that perspective. I just think we get too hung up on who's building the next fastest model, who has it. I think the diffusion here is the most than anywhere else in the world. Patrick, to you, when we've got to do quick answers to quick questions, what could go wrong? Well, being an immigrant, I felt like I should read Democracy in America. So, I just finished it. With the final word with you, Max. I'll try to be less positive than—although for the record I'm extremely positive on this topic and many others. TL;DR

At the San Francisco Fed’s Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference, Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, tech CEOs, and leading economists agreed that superintelligence (SI) is driving unprecedented, exponential gains in software and research productivity, even as macro-level economic data has yet to show a definitive breakout. While frontier firms are already seeing massive returns, policymakers face deep uncertainty over whether SI will broadly augment human labor, displace white-collar workers, or trigger a capital-investment bust.

The Fed’s Framework & Macro Contingencies

  • Opening Context: San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly noted that since OpenAI’s November 2022 release of ChatGPT, AI has evolved faster and felt more transformative than the 1996 internet boom, requiring policymakers to track its real-time impact on growth, productivity, inflation, and labor.
  • Automating Idea Generation: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh explained that while research efforts have increased more than 20x since the 1930s, research productivity has fallen by an even larger amount. Unlike past general-purpose technologies (electricity, internal combustion, transistors), SI could supercharge and automate the creation of new ideas, pushing token prices down ~50% per quarter.
  • Three Illustrative Scenarios: Warsh outlined three non-predictive contingencies developed by Fed Board staff to guide monetary policy:
    • Broadly Shared Gains: SI boosts productivity across both labor and capital owners, keeping real GDP persistently above its long-term average and maintaining near-full employment.
    • Labor Market Disruption: GDP rises above its long-term average, but widespread automation and labor frictions push the jobless rate above full-employment levels.
    • SI Disappointment: Following massive capital investment and equity gains, expected returns turn down, valuations fall, and the economy slows with a notable rise in unemployment before recovering without productivity gains.

Inside the Frontier: Adoption, Productivity & Startups

  • Affirm’s Engineering & Underwriting Gains: CEO Max Levchin reported that AI has made Affirm’s engineering ~5x more productive (with cost per feature expected to drop to 1/10th). Using LLMs to design a new transformer-based underwriting model yielded an 80% performance increase over the non-LLM baseline—translating to ~$2 billion more per year in loans—with zero layoffs due to AI.
  • Stripe’s Startup Surge: CEO Patrick Collison noted that Stripe’s G&A hiring has slowed as a share of revenue, while R&D and sales hiring are accelerating due to higher ROI. Crucially, the 2026 cohort of startups on Stripe is massively outperforming prior years, with new business launches up ~2x year-over-year (unprecedented in Stripe’s 15-year history).
  • Enterprise Bottlenecks vs. Consumer Scale: Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora emphasized that while AI democratizes intelligence for 6 billion people, enterprise adoption is slowed by edge cases. Citing Google’s driverless car project (from a 2009 Lexus to Waymo in 2026), he noted it took 17 years and >$30 billion to replace one human job, and that AI still requires human judgment for the critical 20% edge cases.

Cybersecurity, US Leadership & Market Structure

  • Asymmetric Cyber Threats: Nikesh Arora warned that open-source models like "Mythos" (released 6 months ago) allow even unskilled hackers to find latent vulnerabilities in 50-year-old human-written code, creating a 2-to-3-year "technology rebuild moment" for critical infrastructure like banking. Patrick Collison echoed this, noting that even the heavily scrutinized Linux TCP stack is riddled with exploitable bugs.
  • US vs. Rest of World: Patrick Collison and Nikesh Arora argued the US holds a decisive lead in both model creation and enterprise diffusion, widening the growth gap with Europe. Max Levchin added that while the EU is still debating regulatory frameworks, the US and China are aggressively investing in compute and energy.
  • Who Captures the Surplus? Patrick Collison argued that for the foreseeable future, the vast majority of surplus will acrue to *users* of AI rather than just the frontier labs. Max Levchin cautioned that unlike past revolutions, cash-rich Fortune 100 incumbents are adopting AI immediately, risking an oligopolistic squeeze on mid-tier firms even as solo entrepreneurs thrive.

Labor Markets, Inflation & Higher Education

  • The Productivity Inflection Point: Stanford economist Nick Bloom shared Atlanta Fed CFO survey data showing that over the past 3 years, 90% of firms saw zero employment impact from AI and only +0.1% to +0.2% annual productivity growth (sales per employee). Looking forward 3 years, however, CFOs project +0.8% annual productivity growth, pointing to a major inflection in 2027–2028 alongside high labor churn.
  • The White-Collar "China Shock" & Human Capital: Former CEA Chair Cecilia Rouse warned that unlike the China shock (which hit trade/manual workers), AI targets knowledge workers—particularly administrative roles in monopsiny towns (e.g., college towns, state capitals). Her "nightmare" scenario is that overreliance on LLMs erodes entry-level human capital and creativity.
  • Services Inflation & Relational Jobs: John Levin noted that healthcare and education are "relational" sectors where humans may resist automation, potentially limiting disinflationary pressure, though Nick Bloom and Dan Huttenlocher saw strong disinflationary potential in back-office services and small businesses as token costs plummet.
  • Reinventing Universities & Accountability: John Levin detailed how universities are adapting to AI shortcuts (e.g., dropping problem-set grades, using daily quizzes, blue-book writing, and oral exams). Dan Huttenlocher stressed that machines cannot take accountability, calling for formal verification ("automated reasoning") and new organizational mental models for human-AI teams.
  • Data Infrastructure Gaps: Cecilia Rouse and Nick Bloom urged the Fed and statistical agencies (BLS, BEA, Census) to modernize data collection, noting falling survey response rates, 1-month lags, and a lack of hard data on corporate AI spending.

Predictions & Forward Calls

  • Productivity Inflection: US corporate productivity growth (sales per employee) will accelerate to +0.8% per year over the next 3 years, with the macro inflection hitting in 2027–2028 — *Nick Bloom (citing Atlanta Fed CFO Survey)*.
  • Drop-in Remote Workers: Many in the AI sector expect drop-in remote AI workers (capable of joining Slack/Zoom and doing any keyboard-and-monitor job) within the next 12 months — *Patrick Collison*.
  • Energy & Compute: Two influential AI leaders have a standing bet on whether global energy use will double in a single month in some year over the next 10 years — *Patrick Collison*.
  • Cyber Rebuild: The next 2 to 3 years will be a "technology rebuild moment" as enterprises refactor legacy code to fix AI-discovered vulnerabilities — *Nikesh Arora*.
  • US Growth Divergence: The economic growth gap between the US and Europe will continue to widen due to faster US AI diffusion — *Patrick Collison*.

Notable Quotes

"What might set SI apart as an economic influence is that it could supercharge idea generation. It appears to be changing the method and at least as important the speed of innovation." — Kevin Warsh
"The number of new businesses being launched on Stripe every week is up approximately twofold year-over-year... a 2x year-over-year increase is not something with historical precedent, even for example during the pandemic." — Patrick Collison
"I worry that we are like little frogs as the temperature is going up and that what we are slowly going to be destroying is the human capital in this country because our students are not learning how to use their brains." — Cecilia Rouse
"The average three-year-old learns a language with somewhere between one-tenth and one-one-hundredth the data of the most advanced large language model. Well, that means we're pretty impressive." — Kevin Warsh

What's the reason why if we've got this hypothesis right, which is the Fortune 450 aren't coming along so quickly, what's the reason? Have they not changed their organization, their mental model, their way of thinking, their process, their governance? Help us understand on the diffusion question, not just your own internal workings. Got it. Well, first of all, thank you for having me here. I think it's fascinating. We seem to be focused on talking about AI from an enterprise and enterprise productivity lens. If you look historically, since there was a time about 25 years ago technology started getting built for consumers and not for enterprises. Historically had we built technology for enterprises, the mainframe, etc. When mobility came about and when laptops came about, we started building for the consumer. And I want to go back to something you said. The idea that we will carry genius in our pocket and have access to intelligence at a marginal cost of zero is extremely compelling. And I think that's the optimistic view we have to start with because there's six billion people in the world who do not have access to expertise or people who are physiotherapists and nutritionists. Is all that intelligence going to be carried in the back pocket? So I think that's going to be hugely amazing for society and humanity at some level. Now if you transpose that and say why are we so obsessed with the enterprise version of this new technology? It's because it's expensive. We need to find a lot of money to go build these large data centers required to train these models to get really good intelligence. That's why the focus is inadvertently on how much money can we make out of this technology and back to your point about how can we get enterprises to adopt it quickly and embrace it. I think there are certain things this technology is really good at: processing large amounts of data, retaining large amounts of information. If you have 3,000 people doing customer support, you can have one brain that understands all these interactions and it can be the complement of the human being that's sitting at the edge solving the problem with the customer. So yes, it already has immense applicability in terms of how enterprises operate. But what you're noticing is, as Patrick said, it's really good for repetitive tasks where a lot of analytics are involved, a lot of understanding is involved, but it's still early to give it arms and legs. What I mean by that is giving it agency or giving it independent authority to go act on our behalf. And I think that's where the fear is because that's where the job displacement begins to happen when you can say, "Oh, I don't need you. AI will take care of it." Now, as you mentioned, I worked at Google and not just in sales. I was there in 2009 when I sat in the first driverless car. It was a Lexus with many and I still wonder what the hell was I doing letting it drive me in 2009 or in 2026, which is now called the Waymo. Just think about it for a second. It's taken 17 years since then to take something and replace one human job. One human job has cost more than $30 billion. It's not the mainstay that we worry about. It's the edge cases. I work in cybersecurity. Our products are all about the edge case. It's about that one time somebody will come find a vulnerability, get into your organization, and exfiltrate data. So, it's not the 80% use case we worry about. It's the other 20% that we have to worry about with AI. And I don't think this technology is fully there yet in terms of being able to understand edge cases, being able to plan for those. That is why we still need that human judgment or human in the loop. Now, I know there are certain companies which are off to the races because they found use cases where we need this superior intelligence. I think there are use cases, cyber security is one use case. Superior intelligence allows bad actors to go find vulnerabilities and come attack companies because that requires real smarts and lots of compute. I'm pretty sure it's going to work in cancer research. I'm pretty sure it's going to work in hard science problems which we need to sort of further humanity. But I suspect the benefit of this technology will be over time it'll become the new normal. We will all have access to amazing amounts of intelligence. And I'll end with this. You know in 2004 when I was at Google we used to say search democratized information. Everybody had access to the same information wherever they wanted. And I think AI has the power of democratizing intelligence. So let me start back with you and we're going to go down the line. I'm going to have a couple of individual questions. So when I see you I think cybersecurity, your business is focused on that. How worried should we all be? Well we're relatively early in applying these technologies both you on the business and revenue side for many of us for protection. How worried are you? What are the vulnerabilities to payment systems, infrastructures around the world, and what if anything can we do about it? I tend not to worry, but because it'd be hard otherwise, but this is a harder time than normal because what we've done is this capability that AI has has the ability to find vulnerabilities and bad code and bad things that were written by humans for the last 50 years. And the problem is cybersecurity is an asymmetric battle. The bad actors would be right once; we have to be right 100% of the time. It is very hard when you bring this technology to bear where things which used to take days now can be done with pretty much, you know, it's like what we've noticed in the last six months is there are no people available in the industry who you can call and say can you help me, I'm having a problem. Literally everybody's backed up right now because every company is going through some version of bad actors trying to get into their infrastructure, understanding all vulnerabilities. So the technology which came out six months ago called Midos has now become more commonplace and is available to most bad actors in open-source models. Unfortunately, it's not that the hackers have become smarter. The technology has become so good even bad hackers have become okay. So that's what we're dealing with. So right now I think we're at a bit of an asymmetric situation. We have a disbalance in terms of what we need to get done. There are things which are getting exposed. We will see more cyber events. I think you already see there are more cyber events happening every week than we've seen in the past. I don't think this is going to stop. I think it's going to persist. I think it's particularly important to make sure that interconnect systems understand who the weakest link is. And I think the banking system is one such place where we have to be very careful because lots of people are connected to a lot of different people. And the weakest link is going to determine how safe our system is over time. I think the next two, three years is going to be a bit of a technology rebuild moment. We're going to have to go back and see every mistake, every thing we kind of did not pay attention to, we'll have to rebuild. Now, the good news is AI or SI has a possibility of not just finding vulnerabilities. It also has the possibility of allowing us to refactor code and rewrite code and do a whole bunch of that stuff. So, I think if you take the positive outlook, we have to go spend more time investing in upgrading our technical infrastructure. We saw for a totally different reason the airlines were down this past week. We saw Microsoft had an outage. You are seeing examples of how if you don't pay attention to upgrading old technology, we're going to end up in a slightly worse position than we are. Patrick, since I met you and your brother, you always majored in technology, but you minored in economics. So, let me give you a question that straddles in between. The question for financial markets and maybe for some people in this room is what's the market structure on the other side of this? You were once a little startup company and by your own description you sort of feel like a legacy incumbent after a decade or more. Who gets to make the money? Will the money be made by the big labs? Will the money be ultimately made by the users of these technologies which are those things that could drive that productivity which would be the biggest fundamental change in economics in generations? So what's your sense of what the world looks like in market structure terms? I mean I think that—well actually first let me just echo the last part of what you said and maybe not the first part, which is you said the next couple years going to be a technology rebuild moment. I think that's exactly right. It's what we're seeing across the industry and even the most scrutinized parts of technology like the Linux TCP stack. There was tremendous attention devoted to making sure that it was as secure and as bug-free as possible, a huge, huge incentive for people all around the world to find every little minute error or exploitable sort of caul. And, you know, turns out, it is riven absolutely fount with bugs and problems and exploitable issues. And so I agree with that part what you said and you're intro—I mean this is maybe why you're more successful—but I'm worried. I think it's going to be—we make more money when people are worried. Yeah, so I could be singing, I think it's going to be a mass, and so just that's my Irish sensibility here. But on your question about the market structure, look, I think this reduces to the question of what does the market structure question reduces to the question of just, well, what's the world configuration 10 years hence? Maybe we can make near-term projections about to whom different surpluses might accrue and so forth a year out. But many of you have I assume read the essay "Machines of Loving Grace." No? Yes? Okay, seeing some nods. So this is an essay published by Dario Amodei from Anthropic kind of laying out the positive vision for where AI goes. And I guess I bring these up to say that there's some pretty far out stuff being posited as potential destinations or at least intermediate points in terms of where these trajectories point. And so given all of that, I found it pretty hard to then work backwards, so well, what's the market structure of the cybernetic ecology? Look, I think today and for the foreseeable future, the vast majority of the surplus is being captured and will continue to be captured by the users of these technologies. There is immense productivity gain and new creative possibilities being unfurled. But what the general equilibrium looks like, I'll defer to people here. Max, I won't ask you to define what "fount" means, but maybe in the old country it has particular meaning. Stocks are fount with my logos. Max, let me try this with you. I've been trying to frame this: enterprises at the frontier versus the rest. I might have gotten this from you some time ago. Is SI really driven by individuals and not businesses? Well, I think this is true for most companies and all of us are hanging on to our researchers lest the frontier labs come and get them and overpay them. I think over time this becomes diffused and maybe we care a little bit less. And since we're all on the topic of security predictions, I'll stick with my—I am the optimist apparently on this panel, or maybe the most optimist. Anyway, I actually think that we're going to go through a period of upheaval for sure. There's quite a lot of discoveries of these latent bugs that are being unearthed very quickly by the sort of the likes of Midos. But I think that motion has always been there. It's one of the more fun parts of computer science. And then you're like, "Oh, here's an if statement missing. We'll fix that right now." And what we're going through is an extremely compressed period in time where we're finding all the missing if statements and we're fixing them with SI as our propellant, both in the finding and the fixing. The long-term effect is that we'll build more robust software. The thing that we're getting from this revolution—which is probably the best word for it—is a tremendous amount of creativity that's being unleashed on all of us. The thing that LLMs have not gotten to, and I will take the bear case, they have yet to come up with a single brilliant idea that was not originated with a human. The job changes we're going to witness is going to be all about pivoting all of us towards more creativity. And the real question I think all of us have to ask, you know, how creative am I really? And what am I doing to unleash all of that? And sort of if you're finding yourself devoid of good ideas, that's the moment to worry. But retailers will become better at marketing, more creative at marketing because the fulfillment and price comparisons are all going to accrete towards just efficiencies because these productivity gains will apply to all those areas. And so creativity is going to be the currency of the moment, for security researchers too. Max, let me follow up on an important thing. We'll come to this with Cecilia Rouse and other economists in that panel. What's happening to your workers? What do you expect there to be? You use the word upheaval. What does upheaval mean to your company and to the enterprises you know in terms of your own labor force? So I think in companies I suspect like all of ours to a varying degree, but probably not too different, upheaval is mostly a positive motion. We are primarily trying to figure out where to apply these gushers of productivity. You have some degree of budgeting, some degree of capital allocations we have to engage in even if productivity is just running off the charts because tokens aren't free, electricity isn't free, etc. And so in my world, prioritization has become ever more important, the sort of what is the appropriate risk to take. You know, Black Friday, Cyber Monday is upon us. That's sort of the hunker down part of the year for the two of us. You have to have your 59s or 69s or 79s because retailers expect it, and there's a small army of people saying, "I have this great idea. Let me ship it." And it's a human. It's not AI that says, "I've thought it through and that's the right thing to do." This is the risk I want to take. And the risk is particularly high in the moment before Black Friday. On the flip side, if you ship it and it works, that's another five basis points of growth that you wouldn't have had. So, I think upheaval is mostly judgment and attempts to decide what is the right bet to place right now. And that's always been our job. That's, you know, the thing that brings us to work every day. But the pace of decision-making is increasing. I think what you're noticing and seeing is a gradual reskilling of our workforce. It's not explicit, but it's gradual. Every employee at Palo Alto is now experimenting with AI. We're watching them. Fed’s Hammack Prefers Small Hikes, Sees Risk of Bigger Moves

Bloomberg Podcasts(624.0K)·15:34·2.1K views·2026-11-16
Beth HammackPresident, Cleveland Fed Michael McKeeHost, Bloomberg Radio
